Slides (black), the doctor's notes (green), every gift (red) and the Aldughaither summary (grey, at the end).

Definition, types & pathophysiology

  • Burn = coagulative necrosis of the skin due to an insulting agent.
  • Types: thermal (scald, friction) · chemical (alkali, acids) · electrical — low voltage < 1000 V, high voltage > 1000 V.
  • Thermal is the most common. Thick fluids (oil, sugar-rich) hold heat → deeper burns. Friction = heat + shear. Alkali penetrates deeper and looks mild at first. High voltage → entry + exit wounds, arrhythmias, muscle destruction → myoglobinuria → AKI → admit and monitor.
  • Most common burn in children → scald. 437
  • Electric shock with dark urine → rhabdomyolysis 441; the complication to address immediately → rhabdomyolysis and AKI 441; electrical injury with myoglobinuria → aggressive IV fluids with urine-output monitoring. 442
  • Electrical injury with full-thickness burns at the flexor creases of the arm (deep muscle damage) → keyed fasciotomy. 435 ×3
  • Local effects: vasodilatation, ↑ capillary permeability, fluid loss into the interstitium. Systemic effects (> 20% TBSA): hypovolaemia, immunosuppression, catabolism, loss of the protective skin/gut barrier, pulmonary oedema.
  • Third spacing → intravascular depletion despite a large total fluid volume. Excess fluid worsens oedema — strict balance.

Zones of the burn (Jackson)

  • Zone of necrosis (coagulation) · zone of stasis — viability depends on aggressive fluid resuscitation · zone of hyperaemia — viable.
The zone of stasis is the salvageable one — resuscitation decides whether it survives.
  • The coagulation zone corresponds to a third-degree (full-thickness) burn. 438 ×2

Assessment — depth

DepthLookPainBlistersHealing
Superficial (1st)Erythema only, epidermis intact (sunburn)PainfulNone3 days–1 week, no scar
Superficial partial (2nd)Pale pinkVery painfulPresent1–2 weeks without scar
Deep partial (2nd)PinkLess sensateNo (fewer)Scar in ~2 weeks; infection → full thickness
Full thickness (3rd)Leathery, dryInsensate—Doesn't heal (unstable hypertrophic scar)
  • 4th degree = fascia, muscle, bone.
The deeper the burn, the less it hurts. Blisters form at the epidermal–dermal junction: most in superficial partial, fewer in deep partial.
  • Deep partial → high infection risk → excision + skin graft; full thickness → surgical debridement; lifelong contracture.
  • Most diagnostic feature of a second-degree burn → blistering 439 437; red, painless, blistering oil burn → keyed 2nd degree (deep partial) 439; white, leathery, insensate, no capillary refill → third degree 441; sign of full thickness → thrombosed veins. 428
  • 20% TBSA full-thickness burns of the limbs → early excision and grafting within 72 h. 442

Assessment — surface area

  • Superficial burns don't count. Palm rule — the patient's hand ≈ 1%. Rule of nines. Children (relatively large head) → Lund and Browder chart.
Region% TBSA (adult)
Head + neck9
Each upper limb9
Anterior trunk18
Posterior trunk18
Each lower limb18
Perineum1
  • Use the patient's palm (without fingers).
  • Right lower limb (18) + half the anterior trunk (9) + head and neck (9) → 36% 438 ×2; first-degree arms (excluded) + second-degree anterior trunk (18) + circumferential right lower limb (18) → 36% 434 ×2 435; both upper limbs (18) + the anterior lower limb (9) → keyed 27%. 430 ×2

Inhalation injury & compartment syndrome

  • First, rule out inhalational injury. Hints: closed-space fires, loss of consciousness, difficulty breathing or stridor, facial burns, singed nasal hair, carbonaceous material in mouth/throat.
Suspected inhalation injury → early (prophylactic) intubation — don't wait for airway oedema.
  • First step in a burn patient → secure the airway 441; facial, neck and chest burns from an explosion → early intubation is mandatory 439; inhalation injury → ABC and intubation. 426
  • Clue to inhalation injury → singed nasal hair (vibrissae) 426; poor prognostic sign → carbonaceous sputum 437 ×3; indication for burn-unit admission → smoke inhalation. 426
  • Unconscious after an electrical injury → intubation first. 437 437 ×2
  • Exam trap: some MCQs add 10% TBSA for inhalation injury — the doctor says it's debatable; add it only if the question says so.
  • Second, rule out compartment syndrome (circumferential burns) — 6 Ps: pain, paraesthesia, pallor, pulselessness, poikilothermia, paralysis → escharotomy.
  • Pain on passive stretch = earliest sign; pulselessness/paralysis are very late. Escharotomy runs from healthy tissue to healthy tissue. Compartment pressure > 30 mmHg.
  • Circumferential burn of the arm → escharotomy 437 437; closed-space electrical fire, after IV fluids → assess limb viability for escharotomy. 438

History, examination & referral

  • History: time since injury · circumstances · closed-space fire · LOC · method of evacuation · chemical (agent, amount, contact time) · electrical (voltage, duration) · associated injuries · comorbidities.
  • Examination: ABCDE · general look · consciousness · vitals · local exam (size, site, depth, pulses, sensation).
  • Exact time of injury starts the fluid clock. Jumping from a fire → associated trauma/C-spine injury.
Refer to a burn centre if…
Second-degree > 20% in adults; > 10% in children and the elderly
Any third-degree burn
Face, hands, feet, genitalia
Inhalational injury
Electrical burns · chemical burns
Comorbidities or pregnancy · legal issues · lack of trained staff
  • Indication for transfer → burns of the face/hands 442 442; → chemical burn 439; hot antifreeze on the hand, red, painful, blistered → refer to a burn specialist (hand) 439; teenager with a scald of the face and upper trunk → IV fluids then admit to the burn unit 426; small-town hospital — reason to refer → circumferential burn. 434
  • Late referral of an elderly burn patient — most important prognostic factor → old age. 435

Management

  • ABCDE · prophylactic intubation if inhalational signs · fluids · analgesia (pain-free — strong opioids) · topical antibiotics · optimize caloric intake.

Fluids — Parkland

Parkland: 4 mL × kg × %TBSA of Ringer's lactate — ½ over the first 8 h FROM THE TIME OF INJURY, the rest over the next 16 h. Monitor by urine output: > 0.5 mL/kg/h adults, > 1 mL/kg/h children.
  • Worked example: 70 kg × 20% → 5600 mL; 2800 mL in the first 8 h. Injury at 3 PM, arrival 5 PM → the first half is still due by 11 PM. Burns < 20% → maintenance fluids only.
  • Parkland formula → 4 mL × weight × %TBSA 441; 70 kg, 40% → 11,200 mL 442 ×2; 70 kg, second-degree circumferential legs + third-degree anterior trunk (54%, first-degree face excluded) → 15,120 mL RL 437 ×3 436 ×7; hourly rate in the first 8 h → 630 mL/h. 437
  • Fluid of choice → Ringer's lactate 439 439; oliguria despite resuscitation in a 60% burn → keyed kidney injury from muscle breakdown (myoglobin). 438
  • 3-year-old, 13 kg, 25% burn given exactly 1300 mL RL (Parkland only), unconscious next day → hypoglycaemia (children also need dextrose maintenance) 437 ×5 Gift 438
  • House-fire victim with hyperkalaemia → insulin and dextrose 438 ×7; with hyperkalaemic ECG changes → calcium gluconate first. 441

Topical antibiotics

  • No role for systemic antibiotics in burns. Choice depends on site, eschar and organism.
AgentCoverage / useSide effect
Silver sulfadiazineBroad spectrum (most used)Leukopenia
Mafenide acetateGram positive; penetrates eschar/cartilage (ears, nose)Metabolic acidosis
Silver nitratePseudomonasElectrolyte imbalance
  • Systemic antibiotics only for infection or high risk (elderly, renal/liver failure, malnutrition).

Chemical burns

Chemical burn → remove clothing and copious irrigation with water (≥ 30 minutes; alkali longer). Hydrofluoric acid → also calcium gluconate and ECG (hypocalcaemia).
  • Chemical burn of the trunk and legs → copious irrigation 430 ×2; hydrofluoric acid → copious irrigation for 30 minutes 438; sulphuric acid → prolonged irrigation. 426

Nutrition

  • Curreri: adults 25 kcal/kg + 40 kcal/%TBSA; children 60 kcal/kg; protein 1–2 g/kg/day.
The slide gives 25 kcal/kg; in the lecture the doctor corrected it to 20 kcal/kg + 40 kcal × %TBSA. Use the doctor's 20.
  • Caloric requirement in burns — keyed "70 kcal/kg/% burn" (odd recall; Curreri = 25 kcal/kg + 40 kcal per %TBSA). 438

Skin grafts

  • Meshing expands a split-thickness graft to cover large burns when donor skin is limited Gift 428 438; elbow contracture release → split-thickness skin graft. 435 ×3

Complications & prognosis

  • Pneumonia is the most common cause of death in burn patients; sepsis second. Prevent Curling's ulcer (PPI). Wound complications, scar contracture, cosmetic appearance.
  • 40% burn intubated in ICU, now febrile with infiltrates → ventilator-associated pneumonia 442; vomiting blood 3 weeks after a 40% burn → Curling's ulcer 430 ×2; ulcer in an old burn scar → SCC (Marjolin ulcer). 426

Burn

  • Common types of burns in order:
  • Flame burns (1st)
  • Scald burns (2nd)
Anatomy and Physiology:
  • The skin is made up of the following layers:
  • Epidermis
  • Dermis
  • Hypodermis
  • The epidermis is made up of dead cornified cells that act as a protective layer against bacteria and chemicals and are thickest in the palm and soles of the feet
  • The inner cells in the epidermis are metabolically active, producing growth factors that replicate every 2 weeks
  • The epidermis contains melanocytes which produce melanin that gives the skin its color
  • Humans contain the same number of melanocytes but different amounts of melanin
  • The dermis is made up of fibrous connective tissue and is rich in blood vessels, nerves, and epithelial appendages like sweat glands
  • The dermis protects the body against fluid loss, such as from sweating
  • The dermis contains sensory nerve endings that mediate the sensations of touch, pressure, pain, heat, and cold
  • The skin produces vitamin D, which is synthesized by the action of sunlight on certain intradermal cholesterol compounds
  • The hypodermis is made of fatty tissue that adheres the skin to the muscles and bones
Depth of burns:
  • Depth of burns:
  • First-degree burns
  • Second-degree burns
  • Third-degree burns
  • First-degree burns
  • Involves the epidermis only
  • Erythema and microscopic changes
  • Minimal tissue damage
  • Protective functions are intact
  • Minimal skin edema
  • Rare systemic events
  • Pain resolves in 48-72 hours, and heals without scarring in 5-10 days
  • Example: Overexposure to sunlight & brief scalding
  • Second-degree burns (partial-thickness)
  • Involves the epidermis and some of the dermis
  • The degree of undamaged dermis reflects the subsequent healing
  • Superficial: characterized by tender blister formation, a pink and weepy wound bed that blanches. They heal with minimal scarring after 10-14 days with minimal scarring if not infected
  • Deep: characterized by severe hypertrophic scarring and is prone to blisters and breakdown in the future. They heal after 4-8 weeks and are not cosmetically appealing. Therefore, skin grafting may be required
  • Third-degree burns (full-thickness)
  • Involves the epidermis, dermis, fat, and underlying tissue
  • Characterized by white, dry, waxy appearance and may be difficult to discern from unburned skin
  • Lack of sensation, lack of capillary refill, and a dry leathery texture
  • Significant scarring and long wound healing process
Injury Severity:
  • Depends on the patient's age, comorbidities, TBSA, depth of injury, and associated injuries like inhalation injuries
  • Patients under the age of 2 years have a significantly higher death rate for any given burn due to the following:
    • Body surface area relative to weight is higher
    • Poorly developed immune system and immunity
    • Immature kidneys and liver reducing fluid retention and nutrition
  • TBSA calculation:
  • Rule of nines (see the figure below)
  • Palm rule: size of a palm equates to 1%
Pathophysiology of burns:
  • The principal feature is coagulation necrosis
  • Zones of necrosis in burns:
    • Coagulation zone: irreversible cell death and absent blood flow
    • Stasis zone: viable injured cells and sluggish blood flow
    • Hyperemia zone: Inflammatory response of healthy tissue along with vasodilation and increased capillary permeability
  • Burn Shock:
  • Burns covering > 20% TBSA
  • Within the first 24 hours with marked inflammatory mediators
  • Systemic vasodilation, decreased cardiac output, and capillary leakage
  • Compartment Syndrome:
  • Painful condition that compresses the underlying vessels and nerves, causing hypoxia and malnourishment
  • 6 Ps:
    • Pain
    • Paresthesia
    • Pallor
    • Pulseless
    • Paralysis
    • Poikilothermia
  • Treatment: Escharotomy
Support:
  • There are increased levels of inflammatory mediators (IL-1 + IL-6), with high levels of stress hormones (cortisol, catecholamines, glucagon)
  • Burn patients experience a 1.5-2 time increase in resting metabolic rate as opposed to non-burned patients
  • There is increased gluconeogenesis from the liver, insulin resistance, and muscle breakdown to keep up with the energy expenditure
  • B-blockers were shown to reduce the stress hormone surge and decrease catabolism resulting in protein synthesis and decreased lipolysis
  • Oxandrolone, a testosterone analog, decreases protein muscle catabolism
  • Burn patients are immunocompromised due to the low levels of IgA, IgG, and IgM impairing B-cell function along with reduced T-cell activity
Management:
  • Check patient ABCs with emphasis on the airway, thus excluding inhalation injuries
  • In case of smoke inhalation:
    • Check ABG, hemoglobin, and carboxyhemoglobin levels
    • Give 100% O2
  • In case of airway compromise:
    • Start with attempts of intubation
    • If failed due to the underlying edema, an emergency tracheostomy is indicated
  • In case of TBSA of 20%:
    • Insert a Foley catheter to monitor urine output
    • Establish two large bore IV lines
    • Give IV fluids over the next 24-48 hours
  • Type of fluid: Isotonic crystalloid solution like Ringer Lactate
  • Fluid administration:
    • Parkland Formula: (4 ml) x (weight [kg]) x (TBSA burned [%])
    • Modified Brooke Formula: (2 ml x weight [kg] x TBSA burned [%])
    • ½ in the first 8 hours and ½ in the next 16 hours Urine output remains a main goal of the resuscitation strategy, with a target urine output of 30-50 ml/h
    • Resuscitation is best monitored via urine output
    • > 0.5 cc/kg/h in adults
    • > 1 cc/kg/h in children
  • Start with wound debridement, antibiotics, and analgesics
  • The patient should receive 0.5 ml of the Tetanus vaccine
  • Patients with moderate body burns may be able to meet nutritional needs by voluntary oral intake
  • Patients with large burns invariably require calorie and protein supplementation to reach a daily caloric goal of 25 kcal/kg (60 kcal/kg in children) + 40 kcal/% TBSA and protein goal of 1.5-2 g/kg body weight
  • Vitamin A, E, C, and D, and zinc should be given. Selenium is also given
  • Antimicrobial Treatment:
    • Silver sulfadiazine: Effective against gram +ve and gram -ve. Barely penetrates the eschar. May cause transient leukopenia and is contraindicated in sulfur allergy
    • Mafenide acetate: broad spectrum but poor antifungal. Good eschar penetration is recommended for ear and nose burns. May cause metabolic acidosis
    • Silver nitrate: pseudomonas coverage but causes electrolyte disturbance
    • Silver dressing
  • Temporary skin substitutes:
    • Alternative to topical agents in partial-thickness burns that need temporary coverage after surgical excision
    • Allografts: better in large wounds but expensive
    • Xenografts: same as allografts but cheaper
  • Hydrotherapy use is decreasing, but showering helps in wound cleansing in stable patients
  • Debridement and grafting:
    • Early wound closure is the goal
    • Surgical excision of the wound should be done within 72 hours
    • Excision to the fascia is commonly used when the wound extends to the underlying fat
    • Excision to the viable tissue, known as tangential excision, offers the advantage of providing a vascular base for grafting
  • Early mobilization is essential to prevent contractures and restore mobility
  • Recommendations include joint elevation and the use of splints
Complications:
  • Infection:
    • Most common source in the ICU is VAP then bacteremia
    • Suspect when there is fever, pain, purulent discharge, and erythema of the surrounding tissue
  • Sepsis Syndrome:
    • Second most common cause of death in burn patients after pneumonia
    • Characterized by fever, hypermetabolism, catabolism, and leukocytosis
    • Follow the following criteria with good clinical judgment
  • Eschar Syndrome:
    • Occurs with circumferential burns and trunk burns
    • Severe swelling may obstruct the underlying vessels and lymphatics
    • Escharotomy is required and must be done before arterial ischemia develops
  • Gastrointestinal Bleeding:
    • Occurs due to gastroduodenal (Curling) ulcer
    • Not seen often due to the use of PPIs and H-antagonist
Respiratory Injuries:
  • The major cause of death secondary to burns
  • Carbon monoxide poisoning:
  • Suspect in cases of closed spaces
  • Order ABG and carboxyhemoglobin levels
  • Levels above 5% in non-smokers and 10% in smokers indicate the diagnosis
  • Mild poisoning (< 20% carboxyhemoglobin): headache, slight dyspnea, mild confusion, and diminished visual acuity
  • Moderate poisoning (20%-40% carboxyhemoglobin): irritability, impaired judgment, dim vision, nausea, and fatigability
  • Severe poisoning (40%-60% carboxyhemoglobin): hallucinations, confusion, ataxia, collapse, and coma
  • Levels > 60% are usually fatal
  • Cyanide poisoning:
  • Leads to hypoxia at a cellular level and unexplained lactic acidosis
  • Requires high clinical suspicion
  • Treatment: hydroxocobalamin 5 g
  • Inhalation Injury:
  • When suspected, bronchoscopy is required
  • Signs of airway injury: unexplained hypoxia, hoarseness, swelling of the vocal cords or surrounding tissue on laryngoscopy, and the detection of soot in the airways
  • Treatment: Humidified O2 at high concentration, bronchodilators for wheezing, and chest therapy to mobilize the secretions
  • Mechanical ventilation in the case of pulmonary injury
Electrical Injuries:
  • Electrical current injury “hidden injury”: the passage of an electrical current through the body
  • The electrical resistance of different organs (from high to low):
  • Bone
  • Fat
  • Tendon
  • Skin
  • Muscle
  • Blood
  • Nerve
  • Low voltage current (150 V) results in severe injury
  • The current may go directly to the muscle, resulting in myoglobinuria, which increases the risk of acute tubular necrosis. Alkalinization of the urine and osmotic diuretics are required, along with monitoring urine output
  • Thrombosis and bleeding may occur secondary to vessel disruption
  • The skin burns at the entrance and exit sites are usually a depressed gray or yellow area of full-thickness destruction surrounded by a sharply defined zone of hyperemia along with skin charring
  • Skin is debrided until the identification of healthy tissue, and another look 24-48 hours may be needed to look for deeper injuries
Heat-related Injuries:
  • Predisposing factors to heat accumulation are:
  • Dermatitis
  • Phenothiazines, beta-blockers, diuretics, anticholinergics
  • Intercurrent fever from other diseases
  • Obesity, alcohol, heavy clothing, and amphetamines
  • Heat cramps: muscle pain after exertion in a hot environment, usually attributed to salt deficit and may result in exertional rhabdomyolysis
  • Heat exhaustion: fatigue, muscular weakness, tachycardia, positional syncope, nausea, vomiting, and an urge to defecate. Temperature is usually > 39 C
  • Heat stroke:
  • Temperature > 40 C
  • Dry skin in the presence of hyperpyrexia is pathognomic
  • Dizziness, headache, nausea, chills, goose-flesh trunk and arms, and convulsions
  • Jaundice, bloody sputum, and pulmonary edema may develop
  • Labs (no characteristic pattern):
    • High LDH, AST, and CK
    • BUN and Creatinine may be elevated
    • DIC may develop
  • Treatment:
    • Rapid cooling (Spraying 15 C water or cooling fan)
    • Ice bath
    • O2 supplementation of PaO2 < 65 mmHg
    • IV fluid administration
    • Myoglobinuria >> 12.5 g Mannitol
    • DIC >> Heparin
    • Cardiac insufficiency (hypotension after correcting hypovolemia) >> Inotropes (dopamine, isoproterenol)
  • Prevention:
    • Acclimatization for 2-3 weeks
    • Fluid replacement
    • Protective gear and avoidance of heavy clothing
    • Avoid exercising in hot weather
  • Poor prognosis:
    • Temperature of >= 42 C
    • Coma > 2 hours
    • Shock
    • Hyperkalemia
    • AST > 1000 U/l in the first 24 hours
  • Causes of death:
    • Early: cerebral damage
    • Late: cardiac, renal, or hepatic failure
  • Frostbite:
  • Freezing of the tissues
  • Frostnip, a minor variant of this syndrome, is a transient blanching and numbness of exposed parts (cheek, nose, ears) that may progress to frostbite
  • Managed by rewarming the exposed part
  • Frostbite results: numb, painless, white, waxy appearance
  • Divided into:
    • Superficial frostbite: skin and subcutaneous tissue
    • Deep frostbite: underlying tissues
  • After rewarming: mottled, blue-purple, tender areas with possible blisters
  • Treatment:
    • Rewarming in a water bath of 40-42 C for 20-30 minutes
    • Patient lying recumbent, leaving the area exposed to air
    • Blisters left intact after immersion in a bath for 20 minutes
    • Surgery: only to relieve circumferential eschars if present
    • Amputation: only after 2 months with failure and earlier if infection ensued and could not be controlled
    • If dislocated, reduce after thawing
    • Open fractures require operative reduction, but closed ones only need posterior plastic splints
    • Anterior tibial compartment syndrome in fractured patients is diagnosed by arteriography and treated by fasciotomy
  • Prognosis:
    • Excellent, but at increased risk for future frostbites
  • Accidental Hypothermia:
  • Uncontrolled low temperature of < 35 C
  • Patients at risk: Old people, alcoholics, winter sports players, those lost during cold weather
  • At risk for cardiac standstill, pulmonary, hepatic, renal dysfunction, DIC, and death
  • Clinical features:
    • Cold
    • Pale to cyanotic
    • Mentally depressed
    • Bradycardia but normal blood pressure
    • Slow and shallow breathing
  • Labs:
    • Severe hypoglycemia is common
    • High AST, LDH, and CK
    • ECG:
    • Prolonged PR interval
    • Delayed intraventricular conduction
    • Pathognomonic J wave at the QRS and ST segment junction
  • Treatment:
    • Rewarming (heavy clothes and blankets)
    • Warm IV fluids (heated with heat exchanger)
    • Active rewarming methods:
    • Immersion in a 40-42 C water bath (1-2 C/h increase)
    • Inhalation of heated air
    • Pleural lavage (2-4 C/h increase)
    • Blood rewarming through bypass machine (1-2 C increase every 3-5 minutes)
    • Indications: failed passive rewarming, cardiovascular instability, and temperature < 32 C
    • Endotracheal intubation: protection against aspiration
    • Bretylium tosylate: ventricular fibrillation
    • Antibiotics: pneumonitis
  • Prognosis:
    • Poor when temperature < 32 C: 50% mortality rate
    • Death may be due to brain damage, pneumonitis, heart failure, or renal insufficiency
